Examples of this pattern include dacyxém, uèqtacyxém, geacyxém, ymèqzjyxtacyxém, aqtackacyxém, and kyxaqtacyxém (e.g., kyxaqtacyxém > kyxaqtaczw 'stained glass windows'). However, some -acyxém nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ym, notably tacyxém, acaqaqyxtacyxém, uàacapavacyxém, avgaqacyxém, arèqzkéçtapacyxém and jèqtaqacyxém (e.g., zap tacyxém > avéçym tacyxémym 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Oçtéçapuà are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Oçtéçapuà adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like déçacz and apèqzkéçacz, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ac, éç, yx, èq, z, i, g, èc and some occurrences of à, e.g. zap déçacz ynactavyxap (a beautiful garden), zap déçém àèqeeéç (a handsome man), zapéç déçéméméç oçéçeeéç (a beautiful woman), éméçym déçaczw éçapoçacapaqym (the beautiful children), éméçym déçéméméçym eacyxymèqapym (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -éç to the masculine form, e.g., artacapav > artacapavéç, éméçapaq > éméçapaqéç, jéçtymacap > jéçtymacapéç. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -éçém, -yxém, -èqap, -éçap, -èqym or -acym double their final consonant before adding -éç (e.g., utzéçém > utzéçéméméç, aréçapaqyxém > aréçapaqyxéméméç, dèqap > dèqapapéç, acapuyxéçap > acapuyxéçapapéç, artèqym > artèqymyméç, and dacym > dacymyméç).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -u change to -uàéç (e.g., démacapu > démacapuàéç); those ending in -éçzt or -éçzw change to -éçzyméç (e.g., jtèqeéçaqaqéçzt > jtèqeéçaqaqéçzyméç, oçztyxéçzw > oçztyxéçzyméç), with the exception of the irregular kyxéçzw (old) whose feminine form is kyxéçyxéméméç; -ar changes to -arzéç (e.g., émèqapar > émèqaparzéç); -yxoç changes to -yxkéç (e.g., acuaqyxoç > acuaqyxkéç); -éçoç changes to -èckéç (e.g., dtéçoç > dtèckéç); -éçt changes to -èctéç (e.g., gaqtacaparéçt > gaqtacaparèctéç); -éçaq changes to -ècaqéç (e.g., yxaphzyxéçaq > yxaphzyxècaqéç); and adjectives ending in -èqz have a special form -èqém (becoming -èqéméméç in feminine) that appears before ac, éç, yx, èq, z, i, g, èc and some occurrences of à, (e.g., oçèqz/oçèqém > oçèqéméméç, eèqz/eèqém > eèqéméméç).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -éç, it does not change in the feminine (cf. zap àèqeeéç tyxuàéç 'a rich man' > zapéç oçéçeeéç tyxuàéç 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ym to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ynèqémyx > ynèqémyxym, ynèqémyxéç > ynèqémyxéçym). If the basic form ends in -ym, -w, or -f, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., dacym > dacym, argapgtéçzw > argapgtéçzw, avèqzw > avèqzw), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Oçtéçapuà adjectives ending in -éçacz take the ending -w in the masculine plural (e.g., apèqzkéçacz > apèqzkéçaczw). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -acém, which normally change to -aczw in the masculine plural (e.g., àyxkéçtapacém > àyxkéçtapaczw, uéçapaqtacém > uéçapaqtaczw), with only two exceptions: oçacaqacém > oçacaqacémym and apackacém > apackacémym which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: uéçapaqtacéméç > uéçapaqtacéméçym.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in éméç kyxap tèqzaréç (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are déçacz (beautiful), dèqap (good), dtéçoç (brief), artacapav (big/tall), artèqym (fat/large), oçaczw (false), àaczaq (high), émèqapar (long), dtéçoç (brief), ynéçzapéç (young), ynèqémyx (pretty), eaczkacyxym (bad), eéçyxéméméçzt (best), apèqzkéçacz (new), jéçaqyxaq (small), kyxéçzw (old); e.g., zapéç déçéméméç oçéçeeéç ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Oçtéçapuà, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Oçtéçapuà personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | ynéç
         | 2nd (informal)   | aqz
         | 2nd (formal)     | kèqzym
         | 3rd (masculine)  | yxém
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éçéméméç
         | 3rd (neutral)    | èqap
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | apèqzym
         | 2nd              | kèqzym
         | 3rd (masculine)  | yxémym
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éçéméméçym
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun ynéç occurs before ac, éç, yx, èq, z, i, g, èc, ê and some occurrences of à, it becomes yn'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Oçtéçapuà are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Oçtéçapuà is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ackèqyxt ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êaqtéç ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êaqtéç, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ackèqyxt. Forms of êaqtéç are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Oçtéçapuà, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Oçtéçapuà verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Oçtéçapuà verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -yxymym- between the stem and the ending.

    In jactémacyxéçapaq, the stem jactém- indicates that the verb is jactéméçt (to speak) and the ending -acyxéçapaq marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In oçyxapyxymymèqapym, the stem oçyxap- indicates that the verb is oçyxapyxt (to finish), the suffix -yxymym- follows it, and the inflection -èqapym marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Oçtéçapuà they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    jactéméçt: ynéç jactéméçtacyxym, aqz jactémacym, hz'yxémym jactémacymyméçapaq, hzéç apèqzym jactémyxèqapym, jactéméçf...
    oçyxapyxt: ynéç oçyxapyxtacyxym, kèqzym oçyxapîaqéçym, hz'yxémym oçyxapyxymyméçapaq, oçyxapyxym, hzéç apèqzym oçyxapyxymymyxèqapym...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    kèqzémèqyxt: ynéç kéçzw, aqz kéçzw, yxém kéçzaq, apèqzym kèqzémèqapym, kèqzym kèqzéméçf, yxémym kéçzéméçapaq.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ackèqyxt, êaqtéç, acéméméçt and oçacyxtéç), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éçt (with the exception of acéméméçt, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    acyxeéçt, dacémaciéçt, uàacapaqéçt, éçapkèqiéçt, oçéçteéçt, eacaparéçt, jacymyméçt, jaciéçt, jtèqeéçapéçt, téçaractavéçt, etc.

        For example, for the verb jactéméçt, the stem is jactém- and the ending is -éçt.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -yxt whose present participle ends in -yxymymacapaq:

    dgapyxt, uèqejacaqyxt, avgarzéçtjyxt, oçéméçztyxt, artacapavyxt, àacït, yxapkéçymaqyxt, jèqémyxt, tèqzaryxt, tzaryxt, ymacémyxt, etc.

        For example, for the verb oçyxapyxt, the stem is oçyxap- and the ending is -yxt.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êaqtéç and ackèqyxt, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. ynéç téçaractavéç means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -éçt (all verbs of the first group): -éç, -éçym, -éç, -èqapym, -éçf, -éçapaq.
    Verbs ending in -yxt (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -yxym, -yxym, -yxaq, -yxymymèqapym, -yxymyméçf, -yxymyméçapaq. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -téç (part of the third group): -ym, -ym, - , -èqapym, -éçf, -éçapaq.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ynéç téçaractavacyxym" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -acyxym, -acyxym, -acyxaq, -yxèqapym, -yxéçf, -acyxéçapaq.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -éç and -ym, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "zap oçtzyxaq uèqapoçyxaq", "zapéç jèqyxtéç uèqapoçyxaqéç", "avéçym oçtzyxaqym uèqapoçyxaqym", and "avéçym jèqyxtéçym uèqapoçyxaqéçym."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -g for the 1st group verbs, or in -yx for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -z (éçapaqéçapavtéç éçapaqéçapavz, dèqyxtéç dz, émyxtéç émz, etc. and ymackèqyxt ymz, kèqyxt kz, jèqzkèqyxt jz), -yxym (eéçaqaqtéç eyxym, jtéçapavtéç jtyxym, etc.), -zym (yxapuémztéç yxapuémzym and téçuémztéç téçuémzym and only these verbs), -yxaq (eaczavyxtéç eaczavyxaq, avyxtéç avyxaq, etc.), -aq (verbs in -yxapavtéç : jéçyxapavtéç jéçyxapaq), -éçtaq (èqzktyxt èqzkéçtaq, uèqzktyxt uèqzkéçtaq, èqoçoçtyxt èqoçoçéçtaq and ymèqzoçoçtyxt ymèqzoçoçéçtaq), or éçz (ackèqyxt éçz). 

*Compound Tenses

Oçtéçapuà compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either ackèqyxt or êaqtéç) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Oçtéçapuà, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Oçtéçapuà. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either ackèqyxt or êaqtéç in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "yn'acyx eacaparg" (I ate) or "yxém éçymaq acttyxkg" (He arrived). ackèqyxt is used with most verbs, while êaqtéç is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, ackèqyxt should be used by default.

WORD ORDER

The most common word order in Batizpafçi is the rare object-verb-subject (OVS).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Batizpafçi, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
Batizpafçi has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Batizpafçi, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Batizpafçi article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is tèz. For example, in the phrase "tèz fçimaçu" (the cat), tèz shows that the noun fçimaçu (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is tèma. An example is "tèma kmamitawpa" (the house), where tèma shows that kmamitawpa (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is tèzta for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "tèzta fçimaçuta", the cats; "tèzta kmamitawpata", the houses.)

In summary, tèz is used with masculine singular nouns, tèma with feminine singular nouns, and tèzta with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Batizpafçi.

Before ma, z, mi, w, g, va, bi, çè and some occurrences of çi, the singular masculine article tèz becomes tè'.

* Gender
Every Batizpafçi noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Batizpafçi nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ta (e.g., kmamitawpa > kmamitawpata 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -mag and -zg take the ending -qà instead of -ta (e.g., çugvamag > çugvamagqà 'pipes', czg > czgqà 'games'), except for the nouns tèmapapèmag, tamatitimag, hpazg, and vitèzg which form their plural by adding -ta (e.g., hpazg > hpazgta 'tires').

Nouns that end in -ta, -qà or -e in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., tèma ftiwmiqà 'the cross' > tèzta ftiwmiqà 'the crosses').

Ipogyçàlsh personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). Seven nouns ending in -ru form their plural with -à. These are xûdôbru, ôcôjæcacacru, fæcabru, abæcâlru, ûcru, ôcfru, and âlruâlru (e.g., xûdôbru > xûdôbruà 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ru, such as abæcûlru or vûçru, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ûl (e.g., vûçru > vûçruûl 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ûl, -à or -ûb in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., acôj ôcûçræcà 'the cross' > acûdûl ôcûçræcà 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ôjac typically change to -ôjuà in the plural (e.g., âlruûçôbôjac > âlruûçôbôjuà 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ôjac are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ûl instead. These are abôjac, ôcôjac, ôcôjûçôbôjøôjac, ôcfôjôcôjac, ûhûdûlvæcøôjac, ûçèôcæcvôjac, ûlûdûçøôjac and ûçèxôjac (e.g., acûd ûhûdûlvæcøôjac > acûdûl ûhûdûlvæcøôjacûl).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -ôjæcac change to -ôjuà in the plural. Examples of this pattern include abôjæcac, ôcrûçôjæcac, èôpôjæcac, ûlruûcæcûçôjæcac, vûçôjøôjæcac, and øæcvûçôjæcac (e.g., øæcvûçôjæcac > øæcvûçôjuà 'stained glass windows'). However, some -ôjæcac nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ûl, notably ûçôjæcac, ôjvvæcûçôjæcac, ôcfôjôbûkôjæcac, ûkèvôjæcac, xruøûdûçôbôjæcac and ûcrûçvôjæcac (e.g., uôb ûçôjæcac > ûkûdûl ûçôjæcacûl 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ûhûçûdôbôcf are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ûhûçûdôbôcf adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like abûdôju and ôbruøûdôju, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, e.g. uôb abûdôju âlôjûçûkæcôb (a beautiful garden), uôb abûdac frôpôpûd (a handsome man), uôbûd abûdacacûd ûhûdôpôpûd (a beautiful woman), acûdûl abûdôjuà ûdôbûhôjôbvûl (the beautiful children), acûdûl abûdacacûdûl ôpôjæcûlrôbûl (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -ûd to the masculine form, e.g., xûçôjôbûk > xûçôjôbûkûd, acûdôbv > acûdôbvûd, ûcûdûçûlôjôb > ûcûdûçûlôjôbûd. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ûdac, -æcac, -rôb, -ûdôb, -rûl or -ôjûl double their final consonant before adding -ûd (e.g., ôcûçuûdac > ôcûçuûdacacûd, xûdôbvæcac > xûdôbvæcacacûd, abrôb > abrôbôbûd, ôjôbôcæcûdôb > ôjôbôcæcûdôbôbûd, xûçrûl > xûçrûlûlûd, and abôjûl > abôjûlûlûd).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ôc change to -ôcfûd (e.g., abacôjôbôc > abacôjôbôcfûd); those ending in -ûduûç or -ûduà change to -ûduûlûd (e.g., ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûç > ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûlûd, ûhuûçæcûduà > ûhuûçæcûduûlûd), with the exception of the irregular øæcûduà (old) whose feminine form is øæcûdæcacacûd; -x changes to -xuûd (e.g., acrôbx > acrôbxuûd); -æcûh changes to -æcøûd (e.g., ôjôcvæcûh > ôjôcvæcøûd); -ûdûh changes to -âbøûd (e.g., abûçûdûh > abûçâbøûd); -ûdûç changes to -âbûçûd (e.g., èvûçôjôbxûdûç > èvûçôjôbxâbûçûd); -ûdv changes to -âbvûd (e.g., æcôbâkuæcûdv > æcôbâkuæcâbvûd); and adjectives ending in -ru have a special form -rac (becoming -racacûd in feminine) that appears before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, (e.g., ûhru/ûhrac > ûhracacûd, ôpru/ôprac > ôpracacûd).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -ûd, it does not change in the feminine (cf. uôb frôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich man' > uôbûd ûhûdôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ûl to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., âlracæc > âlracæcûl, âlracæcûd > âlracæcûdûl). If the basic form ends in -ûl, -à, or -ûb, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., abôjûl > abôjûl, xèôbèûçûduà > xèôbèûçûduà, ûkruà > ûkruà), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ûhûçûdôbôcf adjectives ending in -ûdôju take the ending -à in the masculine plural (e.g., ôbruøûdôju > ôbruøûdôjuà). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ôjac, which normally change to -ôjuà in the masculine plural (e.g., fæcøûdûçôbôjac > fæcøûdûçôbôjuà, ôcûdôbvûçôjac > ôcûdôbvûçôjuà), with only two exceptions: ûhôjvôjac > ûhôjvôjacûl and ôbôjøôjac > ôbôjøôjacûl which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ôcûdôbvûçôjacûd > ôcûdôbvûçôjacûdûl.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in acûd øæcôb ûçruxûd (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are abûdôju (beautiful), abrôb (good), abûçûdûh (brief), xûçôjôbûk (big/tall), xûçrûl (fat/large), ûhôjuà (false), fôjuv (high), acrôbx (long), abûçûdûh (brief), âlûduôbûd (young), âlracæc (pretty), ôpôjuøôjæcûl (bad), ôpûdæcacacûduûç (best), ôbruøûdôju (new), ûcûdvæcv (small), øæcûduà (old); e.g., uôbûd abûdacacûd ûhûdôpôpûd ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ûhûçûdôbôcf personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | vu
         | 2nd (formal)     | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcac
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ûdacacûd
         | 3rd (neutral)    | rôb
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ôbruûl
         | 2nd              | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcacûl
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ûdacacûdûl
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun âlûd occurs before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb, œ and some occurrences of f, it becomes âl'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ûhûçûdôbôcf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ûhûçûdôbôcf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ôjøræcûç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of œvûçûd ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is œvûçûd, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ôjøræcûç. Forms of œvûçûd are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ûhûçûdôbôcf verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ûhûçûdôbôcf verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -æcûlûl- between the stem and the ending.

    In ûcôjûçacôjæcûdôbv, the stem ûcôjûçac- indicates that the verb is ûcôjûçacûdûç (to speak) and the ending -ôjæcûdôbv marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ûhæcôbæcûlûlrôbûl, the stem ûhæcôb- indicates that the verb is ûhæcôbæcûç (to finish), the suffix -æcûlûl- follows it, and the inflection -rôbûl marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ûhûçûdôbôcf they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ûcôjûçacûdûç: âlûd ûcôjûçacûdûçôjæcûl, vu ûcôjûçacôjûl, âku'æcacûl ûcôjûçacôjûlûlûdôbv, âkuûd ôbruûl ûcôjûçacæcrôbûl, ûcôjûçacûdûb...
    ûhæcôbæcûç: âlûd ûhæcôbæcûçôjæcûl, øruûl ûhæcôbâcvûdûl, âku'æcacûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlûdôbv, ûhæcôbæcûl, âkuûd ôbruûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlæcrôbûl...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    øruacræcûç: âlûd øûduà, vu øûduà, æcac øûduv, ôbruûl øruacrôbûl, øruûl øruacûdûb, æcacûl øûduacûdôbv.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ôjøræcûç, œvûçûd, ôjacacûdûç and ûhôjæcûçûd), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ûdûç (with the exception of ôjacacûdûç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ôjæcôpûdûç, abôjacôjoûdûç, ôcfôjôbvûdûç, ûdôbøroûdûç, ûhûdûçôpûdûç, ôpôjôbxûdûç, ûcôjûlûlûdûç, ûcôjoûdûç, ûcûçrôpûdôbûdûç, ûçûdxôjûçûkûdûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûcôjûçacûdûç, the stem is ûcôjûçac- and the ending is -ûdûç.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -æcûç whose present participle ends in -æcûlûlôjôbv:

    abèôbæcûç, ôcrôpûcôjvæcûç, ûkèxuûdûçûcæcûç, ûhacûduûçæcûç, xûçôjôbûkæcûç, fôjïûç, æcôbøûdûlvæcûç, ûcracæcûç, ûçruxæcûç, ûçuxæcûç, ûlôjacæcûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûhæcôbæcûç, the stem is ûhæcôb- and the ending is -æcûç.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries œvûçûd and ôjøræcûç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

- For feminine singular nouns, the article is pàwè. An example is "pàwè vàwèsaséyi" (the house), where pàwè shows that vàwèsaséyi (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is pàxsé for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "pàxsé mnwèvèsé", the cats; "pàxsé vàwèsaséyisé", the houses.)

In summary, pàx is used with masculine singular nouns, pàwè with feminine singular nouns, and pàxsé with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Daoximn.

Before wè, x, sa, y, ke, zé, t, b and some occurrences of n, the singular masculine article pàx becomes pà'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Daoximn noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Daoximn nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -sé (e.g., vàwèsaséyi > vàwèsaséyisé 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -wèke and -xke take the ending -ç instead of -sé (e.g., vèkezéwèke > vèkezéwèkeç 'pipes', wexke > wexkeç 'games'), except for the nouns pàwèicàwèke, séwèoowèke, paixke, and wépàxke which form their plural by adding -sé (e.g., paixke > paixkesé 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -yke form their plural with -ç. These are caxiyke, mwèsapàpàyke, nsawéyke, wésaweyke, payke, mnyke, and weykeweyke (e.g., caxiyke > caxiykeç 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -yke, such as wésaséyke or vèoyke, follow the regular plural pattern and take -sé (e.g., vèoyke > vèoykesé 'holes').

Nouns that end in -sé, -ç or -zà in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., pàwè moysaç 'the cross' > pàxsé moysaç 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -wèpà typically change to -wèkeç in the plural (e.g., weykeoiwèpà > weykeoiwèkeç 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -wèpà are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -sé instead. These are wéwèpà, mwèpà, mwèoiwèpèwèpà, mnwèmwèpà, rxsévèsapèwèpà, otmsavèwèpà, séxopèwèpà and otcawèpà (e.g., pàx rxsévèsapèwèpà > pàxsé rxsévèsapèwèpàsé).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -wèsapà change to -wèkeç in the plural. Examples of this pattern include wéwèsapà, myowèsapà, tvàwèsapà, séykepasaowèsapà, vèowèpèwèsapà, and pèsavèowèsapà (e.g., pèsavèowèsapà > pèsavèowèkeç 'stained glass windows'). However, some -wèsapà nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -sé, notably owèsapà, wèvèvèsaowèsapà, mnwèicàwèsapà, càtvèwèsapà, caykepèxoiwèsapà and payovèwèsapà (e.g., kei owèsapà > càxsé owèsapàsé 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Daoximn are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Daoximn adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like wéxwèke and iykepèxwèke, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with wè, x, sa, y, ke, zé, t, b and some occurrences of n, e.g. kei wéxwèke wewèocàsai (a beautiful garden), kei wéxpà nyvàvàx (a handsome man), keix wéxpàpàx rxvàvàx (a beautiful woman), pàxsé wéxwèkeç xirwèivèsé (the beautiful children), pàxsé wéxpàpàxsé vàwèsaséyisé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -x to the masculine form, e.g., caowèicà > caowèicàx, pàxivè > pàxivèx, paxoséwèi > paxoséwèix. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -xpà, -sapà, -yi, -xi, -ysé or -wèsé double their final consonant before adding -x (e.g., mokexpà > mokexpàpàx, caxivèsapà > caxivèsapàpàx, wéyi > wéyiix, wèimsaxi > wèimsaxiix, caoysé > caoyséséx, and wéwèsé > wéwèséséx).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -m change to -mnx (e.g., wépàwèim > wépàwèimnx); those ending in -xkeo or -xkeç change to -xkeséx (e.g., paoyvàxvèvèxkeo > paoyvàxvèvèxkeséx, rkeosaxkeç > rkeosaxkeséx), with the exception of the irregular pèsaxkeç (old) whose feminine form is pèsaxsapàpàx; -ca changes to -cakex (e.g., pàyica > pàyicakex); -sar changes to -sapèx (e.g., wèmvèsar > wèmvèsapèx); -xr changes to -bpèx (e.g., wéoxr > wéobpèx); -xo changes to -box (e.g., tvèowèicaxo > tvèowèicabox); -xvè changes to -bvèx (e.g., saigkesaxvè > saigkesabvèx); and adjectives ending in -yke have a special form -ypà (becoming -ypàpàx in feminine) that appears before wè, x, sa, y, ke, zé, t, b and some occurrences of n, (e.g., ryke/rypà > rypàpàx, vàyke/vàypà > vàypàpàx).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -x, it does not change in the feminine (cf. kei nyvàvàx osamnx 'a rich man' > keix rxvàvàx osamnx 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -sé to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., weypàsa > weypàsasé, weypàsax > weypàsaxsé). If the basic form ends in -sé, -ç, or -zà, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., wéwèsé > wéwèsé, catitoxkeç > catitoxkeç, càykeç > càykeç), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Daoximn adjectives ending in -xwèke take the ending -ç in the masculine plural (e.g., iykepèxwèke > iykepèxwèkeç). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -wèpà, which normally change to -wèkeç in the masculine plural (e.g., nsapèxoiwèpà > nsapèxoiwèkeç, mxivèowèpà > mxivèowèkeç), with only two exceptions: rwèvèwèpà > rwèvèwèpàsé and iwèpèwèpà > iwèpèwèpàsé which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: mxivèowèpàx > mxivèowèpàxsé.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in pàx pèsai oykecax (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are wéxwèke (beautiful), wéyi (good), wéoxr (brief), caowèicà (big/tall), caoysé (fat/large), rwèkeç (false), nwèkevè (high), pàyica (long), wéoxr (brief), wexkeix (young), weypàsa (pretty), vàwèkepèwèsasé (bad), vàxsapàpàxkeo (best), iykepèxwèke (new), paxvèsavè (small), pèsaxkeç (old); e.g., keix wéxpàpàx rxvàvàx ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Daoximn, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Daoximn personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | wex
         | 2nd (informal)   | vèke
         | 2nd (formal)     | pèykesé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sapà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | xpàpàx
         | 3rd (neutral)    | yi
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | iykesé
         | 2nd              | pèykesé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sapàsé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | xpàpàxsé
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun wex occurs before wè, x, sa, y, ke, zé, t, b, ê and some occurrences of n, it becomes we'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Daoximn are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Daoximn is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) wèpèysao ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êvèox ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êvèox, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is wèpèysao. Forms of êvèox are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Daoximn, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Daoximn verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Daoximn verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -sasésé- between the stem and the ending.

    In pawèopàwèsaxivè, the stem pawèopà- indicates that the verb is pawèopàxo (to speak) and the ending -wèsaxivè marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In rsaisaséséyisé, the stem rsai- indicates that the verb is rsaisao (to finish), the suffix -sasésé- follows it, and the inflection -yisé marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Daoximn they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    pawèopàxo: wex pawèopàxowèsasé, vèke pawèopàwèsé, gke'sapàsé pawèopàwèséséxivè, gkex iykesé pawèopàsayisé, pawèopàxzà...
    rsaisao: wex rsaisaowèsasé, pèykesé rsaiîvèxsé, gke'sapàsé rsaisaséséxivè, rsaisasé, gkex iykesé rsaisasésésayisé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    pèykepàysao: wex pèxkeç, vèke pèxkeç, sapà pèxkevè, iykesé pèykepàyisé, pèykesé pèykepàxzà, sapàsé pèxkepàxivè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly wèpèysao, êvèox, wèpàpàxo and rwèsaox), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -xo (with the exception of wèpàpàxo, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    wèsavàxo, wéwèpàwèzéxo, mnwèivèxo, xipèyzéxo, rxovàxo, vàwèicaxo, pawèséséxo, pawèzéxo, paoyvàxixo, oxcawèocàxo, etc.

        For example, for the verb pawèopàxo, the stem is pawèopà- and the ending is -xo.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -sao whose present participle ends in -saséséwèivè:

    wétisao, myvàpawèvèsao, càtcakexopasao, rpàxkeosao, caowèicàsao, nwèïo, saipèxsévèsao, paypàsao, oykecasao, okecasao, séwèpàsao, etc.

        For example, for the verb rsaisao, the stem is rsai- and the ending is -sao.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êvèox and wèpèysao, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. wex oxcawèocàx means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -xo (all verbs of the first group): -x, -xsé, -x, -yisé, -xzà, -xivè.
    Verbs ending in -sao (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -sasé, -sasé, -savè, -saséséyisé, -saséséxzà, -saséséxivè. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ox (part of the third group): -sé, -sé, - , -yisé, -xzà, -xivè.

2nd person     | vèke oxcawèocàxsé        | pèykesé oxcawèocàxzà

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "wex oxcawèocàwèsasé" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -xo suffix, e.g., oxcawèocàxo -> oxcawèocà-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -sao suffix plus the -sasésé suffix, e.g., mnysasésao -> mnysasésasésé-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -wèsasé, -wèsasé, -wèsavè, -sayisé, -saxzà, -wèsaxivè.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb wèpèysao. They are always regular: -wèsa, -wèsé, -wè, -yisé, -xzà, -yivè.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -x and -sé, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "kei rokesavè myirsavè", "keix paysaox myirsavèx", "càxsé rokesavèsé myirsavèsé", and "càxsé paysaoxsé myirsavèxsé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -t for the 1st group verbs, or in -sa for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ke (xivèxicàox xivèxicàke, wéysaox wéke, pàsaox pàke, etc. and séwèpèysao séke, pèysao pèke, paykepèysao pake), -sasé (vàxvèvèox vàsasé, paoxicàox paosasé, etc.), -kesé (saimpàkeox saimpàkesé and oxmpàkeox oxmpàkesé and only these verbs), -savè (vàwèkecàsaox vàwèkecàsavè, càsaox càsavè, etc.), -vè (verbs in -saicàox : paxsaicàox paxsaivè), -xovè (ykepèosao ykepèxovè, mykepèosao mykepèxovè, yrrosao yrrxovè and séykerrosao séykerrxovè), or xke (wèpèysao xke). 

*Compound Tenses

Daoximn compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either wèpèysao or êvèox) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Daoximn, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Daoximn. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either wèpèysao or êvèox in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "we'wèsa vàwèicat" (I ate) or "sapà xsévè wèoosapèt" (He arrived). wèpèysao is used with most verbs, while êvèox is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, wèpèysao should be used by default.

* Case
Nouns in Tîœûgqèté are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Tîœûgqèté adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like oûøcy and gacykûøcy, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ø, û, à, a, cy, sy, zâ, v and some occurrences of té, e.g. cyg oûøcy iøœqyàg (a beautiful garden), cyg oûæ téawwû (a handsome man), cygû oûææû ôûwwû (a beautiful woman), æûu oûøcycî ûgôøgçu (the beautiful children), æûu oûææûu wøàuagu (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -û to the masculine form, e.g., céœøgqy > céœøgqyû, æûgç > æûgçû, xîûœuøg > xîûœuøgû. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ûæ, -àæ, -ag, -ûg, -au or -øu double their final consonant before adding -û (e.g., qèœcyûæ > qèœcyûææû, céûgçàæ > céûgçàææû, oag > oaggû, øgqèàûg > øgqèàûggû, céœau > céœauuû, and oøu > oøuuû).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -qè change to -qètéû (e.g., oæøgqè > oæøgqètéû); those ending in -ûcyœ or -ûcycî change to -ûcyuû (e.g., xîœawûççûcyœ > xîœawûççûcyuû, ôcyœàûcycî > ôcyœàûcyuû), with the exception of the irregular kàûcycî (old) whose feminine form is kàûàææû; -cé changes to -cécyû (e.g., æagcé > æagcécyû); -àô changes to -àkû (e.g., øqèçàô > øqèçàkû); -ûô changes to -vkû (e.g., oœûô > oœvkû); -ûœ changes to -vœû (e.g., zâçœøgcéûœ > zâçœøgcévœû); -ûç changes to -vçû (e.g., àgfcyàûç > àgfcyàvçû); and adjectives ending in -acy have a special form -aæ (becoming -aææû in feminine) that appears before ø, û, à, a, cy, sy, zâ, v and some occurrences of té, (e.g., ôacy/ôaæ > ôaææû, wacy/waæ > waææû).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -û, it does not change in the feminine (cf. cyg téawwû œàqètéû 'a rich man' > cygû ôûwwû œàqètéû 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -u to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., iaæà > iaæàu, iaæàû > iaæàûu). If the basic form ends in -u, -cî, or -e, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., oøu > oøu, cézâgzâœûcycî > cézâgzâœûcycî, qyacycî > qyacycî), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Tîœûgqèté adjectives ending in -ûøcy take the ending -cî in the masculine plural (e.g., gacykûøcy > gacykûøcycî). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -øæ, which normally change to -øcycî in the masculine plural (e.g., téàkûœgøæ > téàkûœgøcycî, qèûgçœøæ > qèûgçœøcycî), with only two exceptions: ôøçøæ > ôøçøæu and gøkøæ > gøkøæu which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: qèûgçœøæû > qèûgçœøæûu.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in æû kàg œacycéû (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are oûøcy (beautiful), oag (good), oœûô (brief), céœøgqy (big/tall), céœau (fat/large), ôøcycî (false), téøcyç (high), æagcé (long), oœûô (brief), iûcygû (young), iaæà (pretty), wøcykøàu (bad), wûàææûcyœ (best), gacykûøcy (new), xîûçàç (small), kàûcycî (old); e.g., cygû oûææû ôûwwû ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Tîœûgqèté, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Tîœûgqèté personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Tîœûgqèté are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Tîœûgqèté is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) økaàœ ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of qîçœû ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is qîçœû, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is økaàœ. Forms of qîçœû are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Tîœûgqèté, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Tîœûgqèté verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Tîœûgqèté verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -àuu- between the stem and the ending.

    In xîøœæøàûgç, the stem xîøœæ- indicates that the verb is xîøœæûœ (to speak) and the ending -øàûgç marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ôàgàuuagu, the stem ôàg- indicates that the verb is ôàgàœ (to finish), the suffix -àuu- follows it, and the inflection -agu marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Tîœûgqèté they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    xîøœæûœ: iû xîøœæûœøàu, çcy xîøœæøu, fcy'àæu xîøœæøuuûgç, fcyû gacyu xîøœæàagu, xîøœæûe...
    ôàgàœ: iû ôàgàœøàu, kacyu ôàglçûu, fcy'àæu ôàgàuuûgç, ôàgàu, fcyû gacyu ôàgàuuàagu...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    kacyæaàœ: iû kûcycî, çcy kûcycî, àæ kûcyç, gacyu kacyæagu, kacyu kacyæûe, àæu kûcyæûgç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly økaàœ, qîçœû, øææûœ and ôøàœû), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ûœ (with the exception of øææûœ, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    øàwûœ, oøæøsyûœ, qètéøgçûœ, ûgkasyûœ, ôûœwûœ, wøgcéûœ, xîøuuûœ, xîøsyûœ, xîœawûgûœ, œûcéøœqyûœ, etc.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.

*Compound Tenses

Tîœûgqèté compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either økaàœ or qîçœû) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Tîœûgqèté, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Tîœûgqèté. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either økaàœ or qîçœû in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "i'øà wøgcézâ" (I ate) or "àæ ûuç øœœàkzâ" (He arrived). økaàœ is used with most verbs, while qîçœû is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, økaàœ should be used by default.

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Érèàçyaçd is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    yaçuehah’er arahluèuérè yl (I love chocolate).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Érèàçyaçd, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
érèàçyaçd has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Érèàçyaçd, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Érèàçyaçd article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is yl. For example, in the phrase "arahérè yl" (the cat), yl shows that the noun arahérè (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ahl. An example is "àçuikwahs ahl" (the house), where ahl shows that àçuikwahs (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ikyl for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ikarahérè ikyl", the cats; "ikàçuikwahs ikyl", the houses.)

In summary, yl is used with masculine singular nouns, ahl with feminine singular nouns, and ikyl with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Érèàçyaçd.

After ah, y, w, u, o, v, b, f and some occurrences of ér, the singular masculine article yl becomes 'l.

NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Érèàçyaçd noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Érèàçyaçd nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme ik- (e.g., àçuikwahs > ikàçuikwahs 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with oah- and oy- take the prefix em- instead of ik- (e.g., oahvoar > emoahvoar 'pipes', oyer > emoyer 'games'), except for the nouns oahehàçahl, oahaçaçahik, oyàçz, and oylàh which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme ik- (e.g., oyàçz > ikoyàçz 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with ou- form their plural with em-. These are ouàçyep, oullwahè, ouàhwér, ouerwàh, ouz, ouérè, and ouerouer (e.g., ouàçyep > emouàçyep 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with ou-, such as ouikwàh or ouaçar, follow the regular plural pattern and take ik- (e.g., ouaçar > ikouaçar 'holes').

Nouns that begin with ik-, em- or g- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., emwuaçè ahl 'the cross' > emwuaçè ikyl 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with lah- typically change to emoah- in the plural (e.g., lahàçaçouer > emoahàçaçouer 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with lah- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding ik- instead. These are lahàh, lahè, lahihahàçaçahè, lahèahérè, lahihwarikyd, laharwèbaç, lahihaçyik and lahepbaç (e.g., lahihwarikyd yl > iklahihwarikyd ikyl).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with lwah- change to emoah- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include lwahàh, lwahaçuè, lwahsb, lwahaçwzouik, lwahihahaçar, and lwahaçarwih (e.g., lwahaçarwih àço > emoahaçarwih ikyeh 'stained-glass windows'). However, some lwah- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with ik-, notably lwahaç, lwahaçwararah, lwahehàçahérè, lwaharbeh, lwahàçaçyihouep and lwaharaçuz (e.g., lwahaç yl > iklwahaç ikyl 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Érèàçyaçd are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

*Personal Pronouns
érèàçyaçd personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Érèàçyaçd are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Érèàçyaçd is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) açwuihah ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of yaçarê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is yaçarê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is açwuihah. Forms of yaçarê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Érèàçyaçd, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

érèàçyaçd verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Érèàçyaçd they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

Beginning of Ijèkhuz Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Ijèkhuz is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    khuçuhym’vy dymçoçujçuij kço (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Ijèkhuz, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
ijèkhuz has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Ijèkhuz, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Ijèkhuz article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is kço. For example, in the phrase "dymij kço" (the cat), kço shows that the noun dymij (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is mço. An example is "èçucfmr mço" (the house), where mço shows that èçucfmr (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ckço for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "cdymij ckço", the cats; "cèçucfmr ckço", the houses.)

In summary, kço is used with masculine singular nouns, mço with feminine singular nouns, and ckço with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Ijèkhuz.

After m, k, f, çu, s, do, x, a and some occurrences of i, the singular masculine article kço becomes 'ço.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Ijèkhuz noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Ijèkhuz nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme c- (e.g., èçucfmr > cèçucfmr 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with sm- and sk- take the prefix q- instead of c- (e.g., smdosdy > qsmdosdy 'pipes', skvy > qskvy 'games'), except for the nouns smhyèmço, smhuhumc, skèçy, and skçony which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme c- (e.g., skèçy > cskèçy 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with sçu- form their plural with q-. These are sçuèkbé, sçuçoçofmj, sçunyfi, sçuvyfny, sçuçy, sçuij, and sçuvysçuvy (e.g., sçuèkbé > qsçuèkbé 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with sçu-, such as sçucfny or sçuhudy, follow the regular plural pattern and take c- (e.g., sçuhudy > csçuhudy 'holes').

Nouns that begin with c-, q- or w- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., qfçuhuj mço 'the cross' > qfçuhuj ckço 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with çom- typically change to qsm- in the plural (e.g., çomèhusçuvy > qsmèhusçuvy 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with çom- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding c- instead. These are çomny, çomj, çomtymèhumj, çomjmij, çomtyfdyckz, çomdyfjxhu, çomtyhukc and çombéxhu (e.g., çomtyfdyckz kço > cçomtyfdyckz ckço).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with çofm- change to qsm- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include çofmny, çofmhuçuj, çofmrx, çofmhufçysçuc, çofmtymhudy, and çofmhudyfty (e.g., çofmhudyfty ès > qsmhudyfty ckhy 'stained-glass windows'). However, some çofm- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with c-, notably çofmhu, çofmhufdydym, çofmhyèmij, çofmdyxhy, çofmèhuktysçubé and çofmdyhuçuçy (e.g., çofmhu kço > cçofmhu ckço 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ijèkhuz are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

PRONOUNS
--------
In Ijèkhuz, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
ijèkhuz personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ijèkhuz are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ijèkhuz is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) hufçutym ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of khudyê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is khudyê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is hufçutym. Forms of khudyê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ijèkhuz, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

ijèkhuz verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ccf- between the stem and the ending.

    In dyèkfmçohumçy, the stem -çohumçy indicates that the verb is hukçohumçy (to speak) and the prefix dyèkfm- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In cèçuccfèfz, the stem -èfz indicates that the verb is hufèfz (to finish), the prefix -ccf- precedes it, and the inflection cèçu- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ijèkhuz they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    hukçohumçy: cfmhukçohumçy kvy, cmçohumçy sdy, dyèkccmçohumçy cçof'sçe, cèçufçohumçy csçuè ksçe, wkçohumçy...
    hufèfz: cfmhufèfz kvy, ckdyîèfz csçuty, dyèkccfèfz cçof'sçe, cfèfz, cèçufccfèfz csçuè ksçe...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    hufçuçosçuty: qskty kvy, qskty sdy, dyskty çof, cèçuçosçuty csçuè, wkçosçuty csçuty, dyèkçoskty cçof.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly hufçutym, khudyê, hukçoçom and khufmz), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with huk- (with the exception of hukçoçom, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

Beginning of Buhfastabi Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Buhfastabi is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    stayoce’è neceqyhybuh sq (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Buhfastabi, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
buhfastabi has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Buhfastabi, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Buhfastabi article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is sq. For example, in the phrase "necebuh sq" (the cat), sq shows that the noun necebuh (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ceq. An example is "faygrcek ceq" (the house), where ceq shows that faygrcek (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is gsq for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "gnecebuh gsq", the cats; "gfaygrcek gsq", the houses.)

In summary, sq is used with masculine singular nouns, ceq with feminine singular nouns, and gsq with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Buhfastabi.

After ce, s, r, y, cu, fu, d, j and some occurrences of bu, the singular masculine article sq becomes 'q.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Buhfastabi noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Buhfastabi nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme g- (e.g., faygrcek > gfaygrcek 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with cuce- and cus- take the prefix zi- instead of g- (e.g., cucefucune > zicucefucune 'pipes', cusè > zicusè 'games'), except for the nouns cuceofaceq, cucetataceg, cusfaw, and cusqla which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme g- (e.g., cusfaw > gcusfaw 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with cuy- form their plural with zi-. These are cuyfasm, cuyqqrceh, cuylarbu, cuyèrla, cuyw, cuybuh, and cuyècuyè (e.g., cuyfasm > zicuyfasm 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with cuy-, such as cuygrla or cuytane, follow the regular plural pattern and take g- (e.g., cuytane > gcuytane 'holes').

Nouns that begin with g-, zi- or é- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., zirytah ceq 'the cross' > zirytah gsq 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with qce- typically change to zicuce- in the plural (e.g., qcefatacuyè > zicucefatacuyè 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with qce- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding g- instead. These are qcela, qceh, qcexcefataceh, qcehcebuh, qcexrnegsbi, qcenerhdta, qcextasg and qcemdta (e.g., qcexrnegsbi sq > gqcexrnegsbi gsq).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with qrce- change to zicuce- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include qrcela, qrcetayh, qrcekd, qrcetarwcuyg, qrcexcetane, and qrcetanerx (e.g., qrcetanerx facu > zicucetanerx gso 'stained-glass windows'). However, some qrce- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with g-, notably qrceta, qrcetarnenece, qrceofacebuh, qrcenedo, qrcefatasxcuym and qrcenetayw (e.g., qrceta sq > gqrceta gsq 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Buhfastabi are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Buhfastabi, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
buhfastabi personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

------------------------

         | 3rd (neutral)    | fay
------------------------
